# Search inside out {#sec-m06}

When the policy text did not fit (\see{sec-m03-policy-text-fit}), we assumed a search that hands you the right policy paragraphs for each question. This module opens that search up. There are two kinds, keyword search and meaning search. Each works differently inside, each misses different things, and the best systems use both.

## Two ways to miss {#sec-m06-two-ways-miss}

Take a small set of eight paragraphs from Tarkika's policies. Two matter here:

- **P2, the hygiene policy:** "In-ear audio devices, innerwear and cosmetics cannot be returned once the seal is opened, unless they arrive faulty."
- **P4, an FAQ:** "Can I return unopened earbuds? Yes. Unopened earbuds can be returned within 10 days."

The other six cover general returns (P1), an earbuds buying guide (P3), faulty items (P5), refund timing (P6), phones (P7), and a sale offer on a product coded AX-7781 (P8).

A customer asks, "Can I return opened earbuds?" The answer is in P2: no, unless faulty. @fig-keyword-scores shows a real keyword search over the eight paragraphs, with two ways of asking.

![Real BM25 keyword scores for the eight paragraphs. Asked one way, the right paragraph comes first. Asked another way, with no words in common, every paragraph scores zero.](/figures/m06/keyword-scores.pdf){#fig-keyword-scores}

Asked as "can I return opened earbuds", keyword search puts P2 first. Asked as "can I send back earphones I already used", it finds nothing at all. Every score is zero, because the question and the paragraph share no words: "earphones" is not "in-ear audio", and "used" is not "opened".

Meaning search, which compares embeddings (\see{sec-m02-meaning-as-map}), would catch the second question, since "earphones I already used" and "in-ear audio … seal opened" mean nearly the same thing. But it has misses of its own. Ask for "return policy for AX-7781". To keyword search, AX-7781 is a rare and exact word, and it finds P8 at once. To meaning search, it is just a product code that looks like every other product code.

So keyword search misses different words with the same meaning, and meaning search misses exact names and codes. The rest of this module shows why, from the inside, and ends by combining them.

## Keyword search: the inverted index {#sec-m06-keyword-search-inverted}

How does a search engine find "opened" among a million paragraphs without reading all of them? The same way you find a topic in a textbook: through the index at the back, which lists each word with the pages it appears on.

A search engine builds that index before any question arrives (@fig-inverted-index).

![Part of the index for the eight paragraphs. Each word points to the paragraphs that contain it.](/figures/m06/inverted-index.pdf){#fig-inverted-index}

1. Split each paragraph into words, and lower-case them.
2. Reduce each word to a common root, so that "returned", "returns" and "return" become one entry, and "opened" becomes "open". This is called **stemming**. It is why the first question found P2: the customer's "opened" and the policy's "opened" both became "open".
3. Drop very common words such as "the" and "can".
4. For each remaining word, record the list of paragraphs that contain it.

The result is called an **inverted index**: instead of paragraph → words, it stores word → paragraphs. At question time, the engine reads only the lists for the question's words. If "open" appears in 2,000 paragraphs out of 10 lakh, it scores 2,000 paragraphs, not 10 lakh. That is why keyword search is fast at any size. Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and the full-text search in Postgres all work this way.

## Which paragraph matches best: BM25 {#sec-m06-which-paragraph-matches}

The index finds the paragraphs that contain the words. Then they must be ranked. The standard formula for this is **BM25** ("Best Matching", version 25), from the 1990s and still the default in most search engines [@robertson2009]. It asks three questions about each word of the question (@fig-bm25-parts).

![The three parts of BM25. Repeats count less and less; rare words count more; long paragraphs are marked down. The middle chart uses the real values from our eight paragraphs.](/figures/m06/bm25-parts.pdf){#fig-bm25-parts}

1. **How often does the word appear in this paragraph?** More is better, but each repeat adds less than the one before. The second mention adds less than the first, and the tenth adds almost nothing. So a paragraph cannot win by repeating a word.
2. **How rare is the word across all paragraphs?** In our eight paragraphs, "return" appears in six, so finding it tells you little. It gets a weight of 0.35. "Open" appears in one, so it gets 1.61, more than four times as much. So rare words carry most of the score.
3. **How long is the paragraph?** A long paragraph mentions many words just by being long, so its score is marked down a little.

A paragraph's score is the sum over the question's words. P2 won the first question because it was the only paragraph with the rare word "open". In code, with the `rank_bm25` library:

```python
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi

bm25 = BM25Okapi([words(p) for p in paragraphs])  # words(): steps 1 to 3
scores = bm25.get_scores(words("can I return opened earbuds"))
```

BM25 needs no model, no training and no GPU. It is fast, it is cheap, and it is exactly right about exact words. Those are the reasons it is still part of nearly every search system.

## Meaning search: embeddings {#sec-m06-meaning-search-embeddings}

An **embedding** (\see{sec-m02-meaning-as-map}) is a list of numbers for a piece of text, placed so that texts with similar meanings get similar lists. Meaning search, also called **semantic search** or **vector search**, works in two stages.

1. Before any question: turn every paragraph into an embedding, once, and store the lists.
2. For each question: turn the question into an embedding with the same model, and find the stored lists closest to it, measured by cosine similarity.

```python
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
from langchain_core.vectorstores import InMemoryVectorStore

emb = OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small")  # 1,536 numbers each
store = InMemoryVectorStore(embedding=emb)
store.add_texts(paragraphs)                             # stage 1, once
store.similarity_search("can I send back earphones I already used", k=3)
```

A good embedding model should place the second question close to P2, because the meanings are close even though no words match.

One rule follows from stage 1. The paragraphs and the questions must be embedded by the same model. Lists from two different models do not live on the same map, so comparing them is meaningless. Changing the embedding model means embedding every stored paragraph again.

## Searching a million vectors fast {#sec-m06-searching-million-vectors}

The simplest way to find the closest vectors is to compare the question with every stored vector. We timed this on 10 lakh vectors of 384 numbers each, on a 4-core machine. It took about 56 milliseconds per question.

That sounds fast, but it does not scale well. At 100 questions a second, the machine would need 5.6 seconds of work every second, so it falls behind. And the time grows in step with the data: 1 crore vectors would take about ten times as long.

So large systems use **approximate nearest neighbour** search, or **ANN**. They give up a guarantee of finding the exact closest vectors in exchange for speed. The most widely used method is **HNSW** [@malkov2018]. The name means Hierarchical Navigable Small World, but the idea is simple. It works the way you find a house in an unfamiliar city: take the highway to the right area, then main roads to the right street, then walk to the door (@fig-hnsw).

![HNSW, as an intuition. The top layer has few points with long links, for big jumps. Each layer down has more points and shorter links. The search drops down a layer whenever it can get no closer.](/figures/m06/hnsw.pdf){#fig-hnsw}

The search starts in the top layer, which holds only a few vectors, linked over long distances. It hops to whichever neighbour is closest to the question, until no neighbour is closer. Then it drops to the layer below, which has more vectors and shorter links, and repeats. In the bottom layer, which holds every vector, it finishes with small steps.

We built an HNSW index on the same 10 lakh vectors and measured it (@fig-ann-tradeoff).

![Measured speed and accuracy of HNSW on 10 lakh synthetic vectors, against checking every vector. A setting called ef trades speed for accuracy.](/figures/m06/ann-tradeoff.pdf){#fig-ann-tradeoff}

HNSW answered in 0.3 to 1.9 milliseconds, 30 to 200 times faster than checking everything. But it did not always find the true closest 10. A setting called `ef` controls how widely it looks. At `ef=20` it found about half of the true top 10. At `ef=200` it found 80%, and took nearly seven times longer. The vectors we used were random-like, a hard case for HNSW, and real embeddings often do better. So the numbers here are only a guide. The right setting for `ef` depends on your own data. To find it, check how many of the true closest vectors HNSW returns on your own data, at a few settings. Module 9 shows how. Building the index also took 5 minutes, which matters when your data changes often.

## Choosing where to store vectors {#sec-m06-choosing-where-store}

A **vector store** keeps the embeddings and runs the search. There are three kinds.

1. **The database you already run.** Postgres has an extension, pgvector, that adds vector search. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch store vectors next to their keyword index, which makes combining the two easy.
2. **A dedicated vector database**, such as Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, or the managed service Pinecone. These are built for very large collections and heavy traffic.
3. **A library inside your program**, such as FAISS or hnswlib. Good for data that changes rarely and fits in memory.

Size decides less than you might think: a few lakh paragraphs fit comfortably in any of the three. Two other questions usually decide.

The first is **filtering**. The pruning step in \see{sec-m03-policy-text-fit} removed out-of-date policy paragraphs before sending them. Better still, never retrieve them. Store a date, a category and a language with each paragraph, called **metadata**, and filter during the search. The order matters. If you fetch the top 10 and then remove the old ones, and 9 of the 10 were old, you are left with 1. A good vector store applies the filter while searching, and still returns 10.

```python
store.similarity_search(question, k=10,
    filter=lambda d: d.metadata["valid_until"] >= today)
```

Store dates in one sortable format, such as `2026-11-05`, so that this comparison works.

The second is **keyword search**. If you need both kinds, as the last section of this module argues, a store that does both saves you running two systems.

So start with the database you already run. Move to a dedicated one when its size, traffic or filtering needs outgrow it.

## The most similar is not the most relevant {#sec-m06-most-similar-most}

Go back to the first question, "Can I return opened earbuds?", and to P4: "Can I return unopened earbuds? Yes."

To an embedding model, P4 looks almost exactly like the question: it has the same words in the same order, with one extra "un". An embedding model is likely to place P4 closest to the question, ahead of P2. But P4 answers a different question, and its answer, "yes", is the opposite of the right one. A model that receives P4 first may tell the customer they can return opened earbuds.

Embeddings measure whether two texts are about the same thing. They do not measure whether one answers the other. Small words that flip a meaning, such as "un", "not", "except" and "only", barely move the embedding. So the closest paragraph is often the right topic with the wrong answer.

Fixing this needs a model that reads the question and the paragraph together and judges whether one answers the other. That is a **reranker**, and Module 7 adds one.

## Hybrid search {#sec-m06-hybrid-search}

Keyword search misses reworded questions. Meaning search misses exact codes and is fooled by near-copies. Their mistakes are different, so run both and combine the results. This is **hybrid search**.

Combining them has one problem. The scores are on different scales. P2's BM25 score is 1.82, while a cosine similarity is between 0 and 1. Adding them makes no sense. So instead of scores, use ranks. The usual method is **Reciprocal Rank Fusion**, or **RRF** [@cormack2009]. Each list gives every paragraph 1 ÷ (60 + its rank), and the amounts are added up. Why 60? It keeps the gaps between ranks small. First place gets 1 ÷ 61, about 0.0164, and second gets 1 ÷ 62, about 0.0161. Without the 60, first would get 1 and second 0.5, so a paragraph that is first in one list would win almost regardless of the other list.

@fig-hybrid works it out for the first question, with keyword ranks from our real search and illustrative meaning ranks.

![Hybrid search for "can I return opened earbuds". Keyword ranks are real; meaning ranks are illustrative. The combined score is shown in thousandths.](/figures/m06/hybrid.pdf){#fig-hybrid}

P2 is first in the keyword list and fourth in the meaning list: 1 ÷ 61 + 1 ÷ 64, about 0.0320. P4 is second and first: 1 ÷ 62 + 1 ÷ 61, about 0.0325. Both end up at the top. For the second question, where keyword search found nothing, the meaning list carries the result. For AX-7781, the keyword list does.

Hybrid search makes sure the right paragraph is among the first few. It does not make sure it is first: P4 still edges out P2. Putting the best paragraph first, out of a handful, is a different job from finding a handful out of lakhs, and it needs a different tool. Module 7 builds the whole pipeline, from cutting documents into pieces to the reranker that finally puts P2 on top.
